---
title: "The Regression Recipe"
subtitle: "Data · Model · Loss · Optimize"
---



Every band in the [next page](05-predictive-bands.qmd) wraps a *fitted
model* — and so far the fitting itself has hidden inside one black box,
`np.polyfit`.  Before we put uncertainty around a prediction, open the box.
Every supervised fit you will ever run — polynomial, neural network,
volatility forecaster — is the same four-ingredient recipe:

1. **Data** — pairs $(x_i, y_i)$ the model must explain.
2. **Model** — a family of functions $f_\theta$, indexed by parameters $\theta$.
3. **Loss** — one number scoring how badly $f_\theta$ explains the data.
4. **Optimizer** — a procedure that moves $\theta$ to shrink the loss.

::: {#cell-fig-recipe-loop .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.6))
ax.axis("off")

boxes = {
    "data":  (0.08, 0.72, "DATA\n(xᵢ, yᵢ)", COOL),
    "model": (0.36, 0.72, "MODEL\nŷᵢ = f_θ(xᵢ)", INK),
    "loss":  (0.64, 0.72, "LOSS\nL(θ) = score(ŷ, y)", WARM),
    "opt":   (0.64, 0.22, "OPTIMIZER\nθ ← θ − η·∇L", CRASH),
    "fit":   (0.92, 0.72, "fitted\nmodel", GREEN),
}
for key, (x, y, text, col) in boxes.items():
    ax.text(x, y, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=12, color=col,
            fontweight="bold", family="monospace",
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.5", fc="white", ec=col, lw=1.6))

arrow_kw = dict(arrowstyle="-|>", lw=1.8, color=INK)
for (x0, y0), (x1, y1) in [
    ((0.14, 0.72), (0.28, 0.72)),   # data → model
    ((0.44, 0.72), (0.56, 0.72)),   # model → loss
    ((0.64, 0.58), (0.64, 0.38)),   # loss → optimizer
    ((0.72, 0.72), (0.86, 0.72)),   # loss → fitted (when converged)
]:
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x1, y1), xytext=(x0, y0),
                xycoords="axes fraction", textcoords="axes fraction",
                arrowprops=arrow_kw)
# the feedback arrow: optimizer → model (update θ)
```

The rest of this page walks the loop once, slowly, on Act 2's running
character — and ends at the observation that ties the whole chapter
together: **the loss you minimize is a probability model in disguise.**

## Ingredient 1 · Data

The character again: 60 observations of a curve, noise growing to the
right, nothing observed in the middle.

::: {#make-data .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
# y = sin(1.3·x) + σ(x)·ε, observed only OUTSIDE |x| < 1.4
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
half = 30
x_obs = np.sort(np.concatenate([rng.uniform(-3.2, -1.4, half),
                                rng.uniform(1.4, 3.2, half)]))
σ_true = 0.05 + 0.45 * (x_obs + 3.2) / 6.4   # noise level, rising with x
y_obs = np.sin(1.3 * x_obs) + σ_true * rng.standard_normal(x_obs.size)
print(f"data: {x_obs.size} pairs (xᵢ, yᵢ)")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
data: 60 pairs (xᵢ, yᵢ)
```
:::
:::


That is all "data" means here: a fixed set of input–target pairs.
Everything the model will ever know about the world is in these 60 numbers —
a fact worth staring at, because the model will happily make predictions at
$x = 0$ where it has seen *nothing*, and nothing in the loop below will warn
us.  (That warning is the next page's job.)

## Ingredient 2 · Model

A model is a *family* of functions, indexed by parameters.  The workhorse of
this chapter is the polynomial:

$$
f_\theta(x) = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x + \theta_2 x^2 + \cdots + \theta_d x^d ,
$$

a family with $d{+}1$ knobs.  The degree $d$ sets the family's **capacity**
— how much shape it *can* express.  Capacity is a dial, and both ends of it
fail:

::: {#cell-fig-capacity .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
x_grid = np.linspace(-3.4, 3.4, 400)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12.5, 3.4), sharey=True)
for ax, (d, verdict) in zip(axes, [(1, "underfit"), (6, "about right"), (15, "overfit")]):
    θ_d = np.polyfit(x_obs, y_obs, d)        # fit this capacity (box still closed)
    ax.plot(x_grid, np.polyval(θ_d, x_grid), c=WARM, lw=2.2)
    ax.scatter(x_obs, y_obs, s=14, c=INK, alpha=0.7)
    ax.set_ylim(-2.6, 2.6)
    ax.set_title(f"degree {d} — {verdict}", fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![One family, three capacities. Degree 1 cannot bend — it misses the curve everywhere (underfit). Degree 6 has enough knobs to follow the trend and no more. Degree 15 has so many it spends them memorizing the noise — and detonates over the data gap, where nothing constrains it (overfit).](04-regression-recipe_files/figure-html/fig-capacity-output-1.png){#fig-capacity width=1484 height=392}
:::
:::


How to *choose* the capacity is a question the loss alone cannot answer —
we return to it at the end of the page.

## Ingredient 3 · Loss

The loss compresses "how badly does $f_\theta$ explain the data" into one
number the optimizer can push on.  The default for regression is
**mean squared error** — average the squared residuals:

$$
L(\theta) \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \big(y_i - f_\theta(x_i)\big)^2 .
$$

::: {#mse-fn .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def mse(θ: Float[Array, "n_params"],
        x: Float[Array, "n_obs"], y: Float[Array, "n_obs"]) -> float:
    """L(θ) = (1/n)·Σᵢ (yᵢ − f_θ(xᵢ))²   [y units²] — mean squared error."""
    residuals = y - np.polyval(θ, x)         # what the model fails to explain
    return float(np.mean(residuals**2))


θ_under, θ_right = np.polyfit(x_obs, y_obs, 1), np.polyfit(x_obs, y_obs, 6)
print(f"MSE, degree 1: {mse(θ_under, x_obs, y_obs):.3f}")
print(f"MSE, degree 6: {mse(θ_right, x_obs, y_obs):.3f}   ← lower loss = better fit (on THIS data)")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
MSE, degree 1: 0.452
MSE, degree 6: 0.073   ← lower loss = better fit (on THIS data)
```
:::
:::


Why *squared*?  Convenience is part of it (smooth, differentiable, convex in
$\theta$ for linear-in-$\theta$ models) — but the deeper reason is the one
this chapter runs on:

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## A Loss Is a Noise Model in Disguise

Assume the data was generated as
$y = f_\theta(x) + \varepsilon$ with Gaussian noise
$\varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)$.  The log-likelihood of the data is

$$
\log p(\text{data}\mid\theta)
= -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i \big(y_i - f_\theta(x_i)\big)^2 + \text{const},
$$

so **maximizing likelihood = minimizing MSE**.  Every time you minimized a
squared error you were silently asserting "the noise is Gaussian, with the
same $\sigma$ everywhere."  Change the assertion and the loss changes with
it: let the noise depend on $x$ — $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma(x)^2)$
— and the negative log-likelihood becomes

$$
L(\theta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \left[
\frac{\big(y_i - f_\theta(x_i)\big)^2}{2\,\sigma(x_i)^2} + \log \sigma(x_i)
\right],
$$

which *rewards the model for predicting its own noise level* — large errors
are forgiven where $\sigma(x)$ is declared big, but declaring big $\sigma$
everywhere is taxed by the $\log\sigma$ term.  That loss **is** Tool A of
the [next page](05-predictive-bands.qmd): "predict the noise" is not a
trick, it is maximum likelihood with an honest noise model.
:::

One more distinction, small but load-bearing: the **loss** is what the
optimizer minimizes; a **metric** is what you report and act on.  They need
not be the same.  We train on MSE, but judge a risk band on its
**coverage** — the fraction of days inside — which is not differentiable
and is never optimized directly.  The
[calibration check](05-predictive-bands.qmd#calibration--keeping-the-95-promise)
of the next page is a metric doing its job: auditing a model that was
trained on something else.

## Ingredient 4 · Optimize

The loss defines a landscape over parameter space; the optimizer descends
it.  For the polynomial family there are two routes to the bottom, and it
pays to see both.

**The closed form.**  A polynomial is *linear in its parameters*: stack the
powers of $x$ into a design matrix $\Phi$ (one row per observation, one
column per power) and $f_\theta(x) = \Phi\,\theta$.  Setting
$\nabla_\theta L = 0$ gives the **normal equations**
$(\Phi^\top\Phi)\,\theta = \Phi^\top y$ — one linear solve, no iteration:

::: {#normal-eqs .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def fit_polynomial(
    x: Float[Array, "n_obs"], y: Float[Array, "n_obs"], degree: int
) -> Float[Array, "n_params"]:
    """Least squares by the normal equations: θ = (ΦᵀΦ)⁻¹·Φᵀ·y.

    Φ[i, p] = xᵢᵖ — each row holds the powers (1, x, x², …) of one input.
    """
    Φ = np.vander(x, degree + 1, increasing=True)       # (n_obs, n_params)
    gram = einx.dot("n p, n q -> p q", Φ, Φ)            # ΦᵀΦ  (n_params, n_params)
    moment = einx.dot("n p, n -> p", Φ, y)              # Φᵀy  (n_params,)
    return np.linalg.solve(gram, moment)                # θ, lowest power first


θ_ours = fit_polynomial(x_obs, y_obs, 6)
θ_blackbox = np.polyfit(x_obs, y_obs, 6)[::-1]          # polyfit: highest power first
print("ours    :", np.round(θ_ours[:4], 4))
print("polyfit :", np.round(θ_blackbox[:4], 4), "  ← the box was this all along")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
ours    : [ 0.0125  1.1502 -0.0813 -0.2766]
polyfit : [ 0.0125  1.1502 -0.0813 -0.2766]   ← the box was this all along
```
:::
:::


`np.polyfit` was never magic — it is these two `einx.dot` calls and a solve.

**Gradient descent.**  Most models are *not* linear in their parameters
(a neural network is the canonical case), and then there is no solve — only
the loop from the recipe diagram: compute the gradient, step downhill,
repeat.  Watch it work on the simplest slice of our problem, a degree-1
model $f_{w,b}(x) = w\,x + b$ with two parameters we can draw:

::: {#cell-fig-gradient-descent .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def mse_grad(w: float, b: float,
             x: Float[Array, "n_obs"], y: Float[Array, "n_obs"]) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """∇L for L = mean((y − (w·x + b))²):  ∂L/∂w = −2·mean(x·r),  ∂L/∂b = −2·mean(r)."""
    r = y - (w * x + b)                      # residuals at the current (w, b)
    return float(-2 * np.mean(x * r)), float(-2 * np.mean(r))


η = 0.05                                     # learning rate (step size)
w, b = 1.6, 1.8                              # a deliberately bad start
path = [(w, b)]
for _ in range(60):
    grad_w, grad_b = mse_grad(w, b, x_obs, y_obs)
    w, b = w - η * grad_w, b - η * grad_b    # θ ← θ − η·∇L
    path.append((w, b))
path = np.asarray(path)                      # (n_steps + 1, 2)

# the loss surface: L(w, b) evaluated on a 120×120 grid of parameter values
w_grid, b_grid = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-1.6, 2.0, 120), np.linspace(-1.2, 2.2, 120))
pred_grid = einx.add("a b n, a b -> a b n",
                     einx.multiply("a b, n -> a b n", w_grid, x_obs),   # w·xᵢ
                     b_grid)                                            # … + b
resid_grid = einx.subtract("n, a b n -> a b n", y_obs, pred_grid)       # yᵢ − ŷᵢ
loss_grid = einx.mean("a b n -> a b", resid_grid**2)                    # L at each (w, b)
b_star, w_star = fit_polynomial(x_obs, y_obs, 1)        # closed form: (θ₀, θ₁) = (b, w)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
ax.contourf(w_grid, b_grid, loss_grid, levels=30, cmap="BuPu")
ax.plot(path[:, 0], path[:, 1], "-o", c=CRASH, lw=1.6, ms=3.5, label="gradient descent")
ax.plot(w_star, b_star, "*", c="white", ms=18, mec=INK, label="closed form (normal equations)")
ax.set_xlabel("w  (slope)"); ax.set_ylabel("b  (intercept)")
ax.set_title("descending the loss landscape", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=10, loc="lower left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![The MSE landscape over (w, b) for the degree-1 model, with 60 gradient-descent steps from a deliberately bad start. The surface is a convex bowl, so the path rolls straight to the bottom — and the bottom (red dot) is exactly the closed-form solution (white star). For non-convex models the landscape has valleys and ridges, but the move is the same: follow −∇L.](04-regression-recipe_files/figure-html/fig-gradient-descent-output-1.png){#fig-gradient-descent width=944 height=585}
:::
:::


Two routes, one destination — because this landscape is a convex bowl.  Keep
the picture: when the [next page](05-predictive-bands.qmd) refits the model
many times on resampled data and the fits *disagree*, that disagreement is
many descents ending in different places because each saw different data.
Ensemble spread is this figure, run in parallel.

## The Same Recipe, More Knobs — a Neural Network

Nothing about the recipe was polynomial-specific.  Swap the model family for
a small **neural network** — stacked linear maps with a squashing
nonlinearity between them — and the other three ingredients do not move: same
data, same MSE loss, and the optimizer *must* be gradient descent, because a
network is not linear in its parameters and the normal equations no longer
exist.  In Keras the recipe reads off almost line for line:

::: {#keras-mlp .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import os
os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "jax"          # Keras 3 on the CPU JAX backend
import keras
from keras import layers


def make_mlp(n_out: int = 1, seed: int = 0) -> keras.Model:
    """x → Dense(64, tanh) → Dense(64, tanh) → Dense(n_out).

    The same idea as the polynomial family — a flexible f_θ built from
    simple pieces — but the capacity dial is now width × depth, not degree.
    """
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed)        # reproducible weight init
    return keras.Sequential([
        layers.Dense(64, activation="tanh"),
        layers.Dense(64, activation="tanh"),
        layers.Dense(n_out),
    ])


net = make_mlp(seed=0)
net.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.01),   # the OPTIMIZER ingredient
            loss="mse")                              # the LOSS ingredient
net.fit(x_obs[:, None], y_obs[:, None],              # the DATA ingredient
        epochs=600, batch_size=x_obs.size, verbose=0)  # run the loop 600 times
print(f"parameters: θ has {net.count_params():,} entries (the degree-6 polynomial had 7)")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
parameters: θ has 4,353 entries (the degree-6 polynomial had 7)
```
:::
:::


`model.compile` *is* choosing the loss and the optimizer; `model.fit` *is*
the loop from the diagram, run 600 times.  Adam is gradient descent with a
per-parameter step size — a better descender of the same landscape, which is
no longer a convex bowl.

::: {#cell-fig-keras-vs-poly .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
y_net = net.predict(x_grid[:, None], verbose=0)[:, 0]
θ_poly = np.polyfit(x_obs, y_obs, 6)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.8))
ax.plot(x_grid, y_net, c=WARM, lw=2.2, label=f"neural net ({net.count_params():,} params)")
ax.plot(x_grid, np.polyval(θ_poly, x_grid), c=COOL, lw=2.2, ls="--",
        label="degree-6 polynomial (7 params)")
ax.scatter(x_obs, y_obs, s=14, c=INK, alpha=0.7)
ax.axvspan(-1.4, 1.4, color=GREEN, alpha=0.08)
ax.set_ylim(-2.6, 2.6)
ax.legend(fontsize=10, frameon=False)
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![The 4,000-knob network and the 7-knob polynomial, fitted by the same recipe. Where there is data they agree almost everywhere. Where there is none, each invents its own story — the polynomial swings, the network glides through a guess — and nothing in the training loss prefers the truth. Capacity changed by three orders of magnitude; the recipe, and its blindness over the gap, did not.](04-regression-recipe_files/figure-html/fig-keras-vs-poly-output-1.png){#fig-keras-vs-poly width=1184 height=440}
:::
:::


This is the model family the [next page](05-predictive-bands.qmd) builds
its uncertainty around — and the figure already whispers why uncertainty is
needed: two models, equally happy on the training data, telling different
stories everywhere else.

## Choosing Capacity — The Loss Can't Do It Alone

Back to the dial that the loss cannot set.  Training loss *always* falls as
capacity rises — a degree-59 polynomial threads all 60 points and scores
zero.  The number that tells the truth is the error on data the fit **never
saw**.  Hold out every other point and ask both numbers, across the whole
dial:

::: {#cell-fig-capacity-ucurve .cell execution_count=10}
``` {.python .cell-code}
train_idx = np.arange(x_obs.size) % 2 == 0   # every other point trains…
val_idx = ~train_idx                         # …the rest only judges

degrees = np.arange(1, 17)
rmse_train, rmse_val = [], []
for d in degrees:
    θ_d = np.polyfit(x_obs[train_idx], y_obs[train_idx], d)
    pred_train = np.polyval(θ_d, x_obs[train_idx])
    pred_val = np.polyval(θ_d, x_obs[val_idx])
    rmse_train.append(np.sqrt(np.mean((y_obs[train_idx] - pred_train)**2)))
    rmse_val.append(np.sqrt(np.mean((y_obs[val_idx] - pred_val)**2)))

best_d = degrees[int(np.argmin(rmse_val))]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.8))
ax.plot(degrees, rmse_train, "-o", c=COOL, ms=5, label="train RMSE (seen data)")
ax.plot(degrees, rmse_val, "-o", c=CRASH, ms=5, label="held-out RMSE (unseen data)")
ax.axvline(best_d, color=INK, lw=1.2, ls="--")
ax.annotate(f"best capacity ≈ degree {best_d}", (best_d, max(rmse_val) * 0.7),
            xytext=(8, 0), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=10)
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("polynomial degree (capacity)"); ax.set_ylabel("RMSE  [y units]")
ax.legend(fontsize=10, frameon=False); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Train error falls forever as capacity grows — that is memorization, not learning. Held-out error traces the honest curve: falling while added capacity captures real structure, then turning up when the extra knobs start fitting noise. The minimum is the right capacity for THIS amount of data and THIS split — the exact winner wobbles between runs (here 9, near the capacity figure's degree-6 ballpark), but the shape of the curve never does.](04-regression-recipe_files/figure-html/fig-capacity-ucurve-output-1.png){#fig-capacity-ucurve width=1063 height=441}
:::
:::


This is the recipe's fifth ingredient hiding in plain sight: **evaluation on
unseen data**.  It is also where this page hands off.  The held-out curve
says *how wrong* the model is on average — one number for the whole x-axis.
The [next page](05-predictive-bands.qmd) asks the sharper question this
chapter exists for: how wrong is it **here, at this $x$** — and how much of
that wrongness is the world's noise ($\sigma(x)$, a *loss term* as we saw
above) versus the model's own ignorance (forty descents disagreeing)?

::: {.eli5}
**One-liner recap.**  Data is fixed, parameters move: the model predicts,
the loss scores, the optimizer descends — and the loss you chose was a noise
model all along, which is why putting honest uncertainty around the fit is a
continuation of fitting, not a new subject.
:::
